Monasticism is the practice of leaving ordinary society behind and dedicating one's entire life to spiritual or religious purposes, usually by following a strict set of rules and disciplines. It is the collective word for the whole tradition, lifestyle, and institution surrounding this way of living.

Think of it this way: most people live in the "outside world" — they have jobs, families, social lives, money, and everyday pleasures. A person who chooses monasticism deliberately steps away from all of that and says, "I want my entire existence to revolve around my faith, my spiritual growth, and nothing else."

The people who practice monasticism are called monks (men) and nuns (women). The places where they live are called monasteries (for monks) or convents/nunneries (for nuns).
What monasticism actually looks like in practice

A monastic life is built around three central ideas:

1. Withdrawal from the world.
A person who enters monastic life steps back from ordinary society. This doesn't always mean they never leave their monastery — but it means the outside world, with its distractions, temptations, and noise, is no longer the center of their life. Their spiritual life is.

2. A strict, structured daily routine.
Monastic life is deeply disciplined. Every hour of the day tends to be assigned a purpose — times for prayer, meditation, study, work, eating, and sleeping. There is very little room for idleness or personal whims. This structure exists because monasticism teaches that an undisciplined life leads the mind away from spiritual growth.

3. Formal vows and commitments.
People who enter monasticism typically take solemn vows — binding promises they make before God or their spiritual community. The most common vows across different traditions are:

  • Celibacy — choosing never to marry or engage in sexual relationships, so that no romantic attachment diverts their focus.
  • Poverty — giving up personal ownership of money and possessions, often pooling everything communally.
  • Obedience — submitting to the authority of a spiritual leader (like an abbot or abbess) and the rules of their order, surrendering personal self-will.

These three vows together are designed to cut away the three biggest anchors that tie a person to "the world": desire (sexual/romantic), greed (material things), and ego (the need to be in charge of one's own life).
The two main forms monasticism takes

Monasticism is not one-size-fits-all. Historically, it has taken two distinct shapes:

Communal monasticism (called cenobitic monasticism):
This is the most common form. Monks or nuns live together in a community inside a monastery. They pray together, eat together, work together, and follow the same rules together. Each member of the community surrenders their individuality to the group's shared spiritual mission. This type gives people mutual support, accountability, and structure.

Solitary monasticism (called eremitic monasticism):
Here, a person lives alone — usually in a remote cave, forest, desert, or small cell. These individuals are called hermits or anchorites. They seek God or enlightenment in complete silence and isolation. This is the more extreme, radical form of monasticism. Think of a lone monk meditating in a Himalayan cave — that is eremitic monasticism.

There is also a semi-eremitic middle ground, where small groups of hermits live near each other but largely alone, coming together only for certain prayers or meals.

Monasticism is not exclusive to one religion. It appears across several of the world's great faiths, though it looks different in each:

Christianity:
Monasticism has a long and rich history in both Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christianity. Christian monks and nuns live in monasteries, follow written rules (the most famous being the Rule of Saint Benedict), and divide their day between communal prayer (called the Divine Office or Liturgy of the Hours), manual labor, and study. Famous monastic orders include the Benedictines, Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Trappists.

Buddhism:
Buddhist monasticism is arguably the oldest continuously practiced form of monasticism in the world. Buddhist monks (called bhikkhus) and nuns (bhikkhunis) shave their heads, wear robes, give up all possessions, and depend on the lay community for food (often through daily alms rounds). They dedicate their lives to following the Buddha's teachings, meditating, and working toward enlightenment and the end of suffering. Buddhist monasticism is especially prominent in countries like Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Tibet, Japan, and Korea.

Hinduism:
In Hinduism, monasticism takes the form of sannyasa — a stage of life where a person formally renounces the world. A sannyasi (male renunciant) or sannyasini (female renunciant) gives up home, family, and possessions to wander and seek union with the divine (Brahman). Some Hindu monks live in organized monasteries called mathas.

Jainism:
Jain monasticism is among the strictest in the world. Jain monks and nuns follow extreme non-violence (ahimsa) — some even avoid wearing clothes so as not to harm any creature in the making of fabric, and carry a small broom to gently sweep insects from their path before walking.

Taoism and other traditions:
Taoism also has monastic communities, though they are less widely known in the West. Various other traditions have their own forms of monasticism too.

This is an important question, because from the outside, the monastic life looks like one of extreme sacrifice. Why would anyone willingly give up family, romance, money, and freedom?

The answer lies in what monasticism promises in return. Those who enter it believe that ordinary life — with its endless chasing after pleasure, money, status, and relationships — ultimately leads to restlessness, suffering, and a feeling of emptiness. Monasticism offers a deliberate alternative: a life stripped of all distraction, where the only pursuit is the deepest one — knowing God, achieving enlightenment, or realizing ultimate truth.

Monastic traditions also teach that spiritual growth requires sustained effort over a lifetime, not occasional prayer or weekend retreats. You simply cannot go deep enough if you are also busy paying bills, raising children, managing relationships, and navigating social life. Monasticism clears all of that away so the pursuit of the sacred can be total and uncompromised.

Additionally, many monastics feel a powerful inner calling — a sense that this is simply what they are meant to do, not a sacrifice but a fulfillment.
What monasticism contributes beyond the monastery walls

Here is something often overlooked: monasticism has had an enormous impact on the world outside monastery walls.

Throughout history, monasteries were centers of education, literacy, and learning — in medieval Europe, monks were often the only people preserving ancient texts by hand-copying them. Monasteries ran hospitals and cared for the sick and poor. They developed agriculture, produced wine, cheese, beer, and herbs. They built architecture of lasting beauty. Buddhist monasteries served as universities and centers of philosophy in Asia.

Monastic communities also served (and still serve) as spiritual resources for ordinary people — places of retreat, pilgrimage, and prayer that the wider society could draw on.

If you had to summarize the entire word in one sentence:

Monasticism is the organized, rule-bound, and vow-driven way of life in which individuals withdraw from ordinary society to devote themselves completely to spiritual or religious practice, either alone or in community.

Every other detail about the word — the different religions, the different forms, the vows, the history, the purpose — is simply an elaboration of that core idea.
